title: Week 6 · Lesson 18: Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 6 — Lesson 18: Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal

Use liver synthetic/excretory functions, biliary flow, pancreatic inflammation, and portal hemodynamics to approach jaundice, abnormal liver tests, RUQ/epigastric pain, ascites, and altered mental status—while recognizing cholangitis, acute pancreatitis, GI bleeding, and decompensated cirrhosis emergencies.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, and impaired liver synthetic function.
  • Explain bilirubin handling and the clinical logic of jaundice, dark urine, and pale stool.
  • Connect cirrhosis to portal hypertension, ascites, variceal bleeding, and encephalopathy.
  • Recognize biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, and gallstone pancreatitis patterns.
  • Build a safe initial evaluation and disposition plan for hepatobiliary and pancreatic presentations.

Part 1 — The liver is a metabolic, synthetic, and excretory organ

The liver processes nutrients and medications, produces albumin and clotting factors, converts ammonia and other toxins, and excretes bilirubin through bile. When liver disease progresses, the clinical problems extend beyond “elevated enzymes”: coagulopathy, edema/ascites, encephalopathy, hypoglycemia risk, infection susceptibility, portal hypertension, and GI bleeding can occur.

For abnormal liver tests, first ask what pattern is present: hepatocellular injury (aminotransferase-predominant), cholestatic/biliary pattern (alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin-predominant), or impaired synthetic function (albumin/coagulation abnormalities). Interpret trends, medication/supplement exposure, alcohol, metabolic risk, viral risk, symptoms, and imaging context together.

Part 2 — Bilirubin and jaundice

Bilirubin is produced during heme breakdown, processed by the liver, and excreted into bile. Jaundice can arise before the liver (excess production such as hemolysis), within the liver (hepatocellular dysfunction), or after the liver (biliary obstruction). Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble; obstruction can lead to dark urine and reduced bilirubin reaching the intestine, producing pale stools.

Jaundice is a sign, not a diagnosis. Fever, RUQ pain, hypotension, confusion, pruritus, weight loss, dark urine, pale stool, and medication history help determine urgency and differential.

Part 3 — Steatotic liver disease and chronic injury

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is strongly associated with insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, and may be silent for years. Alcohol-associated injury, chronic viral hepatitis, autoimmune disease, medication toxicity, and genetic/metabolic disorders also contribute to chronic liver damage. Persistent injury activates inflammation and fibrogenesis; fibrosis can progress to cirrhosis.

Part 4 — Cirrhosis and portal hypertension

Cirrhosis is permanent scarring that disrupts normal hepatic architecture and increases resistance to portal blood flow. Portal hypertension drives collateral venous formation, including esophageal/gastric varices, and contributes to ascites and splenomegaly. Reduced hepatic synthesis can lower albumin and clotting-factor production; impaired detoxification can contribute to encephalopathy.

Decompensation includes ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, jaundice, infection, and renal dysfunction. New confusion or personality change in a patient with advanced liver disease requires assessment for encephalopathy and precipitants such as infection, bleeding, dehydration, constipation, medications, or electrolyte disturbance—but other neurologic emergencies remain in the differential.

Part 5 — Ascites is not a diagnosis

Ascites can result from portal hypertension, but heart failure, malignancy, infection, nephrotic states, and other conditions may also contribute. A patient with cirrhosis and new/worsening ascites, fever, abdominal pain/tenderness, hypotension, kidney injury, or altered mentation needs urgent evaluation for infection and decompensation. Do not assume all abdominal distention in liver disease is benign fluid retention.

Part 6 — Gallstones and biliary obstruction

Gallstones may be silent. When a stone transiently obstructs cystic-duct outflow, biliary colic can cause episodic RUQ or epigastric pain, often after meals. Persistent obstruction and inflammation can produce acute cholecystitis. Obstruction of the common bile duct can cause jaundice and cholestasis; obstruction with infection of the biliary tree is cholangitis.

RUQ/epigastric pain with fever/chills and jaundice is a dangerous cholangitis pattern. Add hypotension or altered mentation and the risk is even higher. This requires emergency evaluation; do not manage presumed biliary infection with routine outpatient observation.

Part 7 — Acute pancreatitis

Acute pancreatitis is pancreatic inflammation and autodigestive injury. Common causes include gallstones and alcohol, but metabolic factors, medications, procedures, and other causes matter. Typical presentation is persistent severe epigastric pain that may radiate to the back with nausea/vomiting. Diagnosis integrates symptoms, examination, and laboratory/imaging findings; lipase supports but does not replace clinical reasoning.

Severe pain, persistent vomiting, dehydration, hypotension, hypoxemia, fever, jaundice, altered mental status, or systemic inflammatory signs warrant emergency evaluation. Gallstone pancreatitis links biliary obstruction directly to pancreatic disease.

Part 8 — Focused exam and diagnostics

Assess appearance, vitals, jaundice, mental status, volume status, abdominal distention, focal tenderness/guarding, hepatosplenomegaly, edema, stigmata of chronic liver disease, and evidence of GI bleeding. Targeted testing can include CBC, metabolic panel, hepatic tests, bilirubin fractionation, coagulation studies, lipase, pregnancy test when relevant, viral/autoimmune studies, and imaging. RUQ ultrasound often helps evaluate gallbladder, biliary dilation, and liver architecture; imaging choice depends on the clinical question and stability.

Case 1 — Jaundice with infection concern

A patient has RUQ pain, fever/chills, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Think obstructed/infected biliary tract, not isolated “abnormal liver tests.” This is a potentially life-threatening cholangitis presentation requiring emergency care.

Case 2 — Decompensated cirrhosis

A patient with cirrhosis develops increasing ascites, confusion, and black stools. Portal hypertension may have produced varices, bleeding can trigger encephalopathy, and infection/renal dysfunction are also concerns. Immediate assessment and hospital-level evaluation are needed.

Case 3 — Epigastric pain to the back

A patient has persistent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting after a biliary episode. Acute pancreatitis, including gallstone pancreatitis, is a key concern. Evaluate urgently for systemic severity and obstruction.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Identify the dominant syndrome: hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, synthetic failure, portal hypertension, biliary pain/infection, or pancreatitis.
  2. Assess stability: vitals, mental status, bleeding, peritoneal signs, oxygenation, and hydration.
  3. Use bilirubin pattern, liver tests, coagulation/synthesis, lipase, and imaging to answer specific questions.
  4. Look for triggers: alcohol, metabolic disease, viral risk, medication/supplements, gallstones, infection, and bleeding.
  5. Escalate urgently for cholangitis, severe pancreatitis, GI/variceal bleeding, shock, encephalopathy, or decompensated cirrhosis.

High-Yield Summary

Jaundice: prehepatic, hepatocellular, or obstructive; dark urine/pale stool suggest conjugated biliary obstruction.
Cirrhosis: fibrosis → portal hypertension, ascites, varices, encephalopathy, synthetic dysfunction.
Cholangitis: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice is an emergency pattern.
Pancreatitis: persistent severe epigastric pain often radiating to back; gallstones and alcohol are common causes.
Red flags: shock, confusion, hematemesis/melena, fever with jaundice/RUQ pain, severe persistent pain/vomiting, hypoxemia, or peritoneal signs require emergency care.
